power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("ps>.05", "ps>.05"), Sentence = c("No significant caregiver-participant differences were observed for the remaining subscales or items (all ps>.05).", "Associations for remaining sleep pattern variables were nonsignificant (all ps>.05), with coefficients ranging from ρ=-.22 to .58, reflecting weak negative to moderate positive associations." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Julia Foksinska and Jacob Moore, individuals with Down syndrome; Melissa Haughery, Executive Director of the Down Syndrome of Alabama and mother of a child with Down syndrome; Dana Sciullo, former Health Programs Coordinator of the National Down Syndrome Society and sister of an adult with Down syndrome; David Lang, Vice President of Programs at The Exceptional Foundation; Snehal Khatri MD, developmental-behavioral pediatrician and Medical Director of the UAB Lifespan Down Syndrome Clinic; Mohini Gunnett MD, pediatric pulmonologist and sleep medicine specialist at the Sleep Disorders Center at Children's of Alabama; and Mary Halsey Maddox MD, pediatrician and sleep medicine specialist and founder of Sleep Dreams Coaching.

Their contributions informed the tailoring of self-report measures for youth with Down syndrome, recruitment strategies, the development of visual materials, and the use of clear and accessible language.
Their perspectives helped ensure that the study materials were responsive to the needs and experiences of youth with Down syndrome and their families.

Down syndrome (DS), a genetic condition caused by trisomy 21, is associated with mild to moderate intellectual disability (ID) and substantial variability in cognitive, emotional, and behavioral functioning (Antonarakis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Down syndrome (DS), a genetic condition caused by trisomy 21, is associated with mild to moderate intellectual disability (ID) and substantial variability in cognitive, emotional, and behavioral functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Antonarakis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Sleep problems represent a significant concern for daily functioning and quality of life across the lifespan in individuals with DS due to elevated rates of insomnia, nighttime awakenings, and obstructive sleep apnea (Carter et al., 2009; Hoffmire et al., 2014; Horne et al., 2023; Maris et al., 201).
text.formatted: Sleep problems represent a significant concern for daily functioning and quality of life across the lifespan in individuals with DS due to elevated rates of insomnia, nighttime awakenings, and obstructive sleep apnea <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Carter et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Hoffmire et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Horne et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Maris et al., 201)</ref>.

text.text: Among children with DS, rates of sleep problems including daytime sleepiness, bedtime resistance, restlessness during sleep, night waking, not falling asleep in own bed, and bedwetting range from 25% to 70% (Fucà et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Among children with DS, rates of sleep problems including daytime sleepiness, bedtime resistance, restlessness during sleep, night waking, not falling asleep in own bed, and bedwetting range from 25% to 70% <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Fucà et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In adults with DS, prevalence rates of sleep problems range from 13 to 86% (Giménez et al., 2021), although information on these prevalence rates is limited.
text.formatted: In adults with DS, prevalence rates of sleep problems range from 13 to 86% <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Giménez et al., 2021)</ref>, although information on these prevalence rates is limited.

text.text: Higher rates of insomnia and related sleep problems among older adults indicate some sleep problems are in part agerelated (Cody et al., 2020; Esbensen, 2016).
text.formatted: Higher rates of insomnia and related sleep problems among older adults indicate some sleep problems are in part agerelated <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cody et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Esbensen, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, the prevalence of sleep problems such as bedtime resistance, restlessness during sleep, night waking, not falling asleep in own bed, bedwetting, and subsequent daytime sleepiness, are not well documented among young people with DS (Giménez et al., 2021; Stores, 2019).
text.formatted: However, the prevalence of sleep problems such as bedtime resistance, restlessness during sleep, night waking, not falling asleep in own bed, bedwetting, and subsequent daytime sleepiness, are not well documented among young people with DS <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Giménez et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Stores, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond age-related differences, sex may also play an important role in predicting sleep problems in young people with DS.

While some evidence suggests adolescent boys with DS experience more sleep disordered breathing and daytime sleepiness than girls (Fucà et al., 2021; Maris et al., 2016), findings among adults are inconsistent (Giménez et al., 2018; Moriyama et al., 2018; Stores, 2019).
text.formatted: While some evidence suggests adolescent boys with DS experience more sleep disordered breathing and daytime sleepiness than girls <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Fucà et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Maris et al., 2016)</ref>, findings among adults are inconsistent <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Giménez et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Moriyama et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Stores, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: One study reported more severe daytime sleepiness and more frequent napping in males compared to females (Moriyama et al., 2018), while other studies report no significant sex differences in both self-reported and objective measures of sleep problems (Giménez et al., 2018; Stores, 2019).
text.formatted: One study reported more severe daytime sleepiness and more frequent napping in males compared to females <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Moriyama et al., 2018)</ref>, while other studies report no significant sex differences in both self-reported and objective measures of sleep problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Giménez et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Stores, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These mixed findings highlight the need for additional research examining both age and sex in relation to sleep problems among young people with DS.
Accurate assessment of sleep in individuals with DS also presents important challenges.
Although sleep is typically assessed using caregiver report, caregivers may have limited awareness of subjective sleep experiences such as sleep quality, night awakenings, or perceived restfulness.
Caregiver-report and objective measures often yield discrepant findings, and agreement between caregiver and self-report has rarely been examined (Giménez et al., 2018; Horne et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Caregiver-report and objective measures often yield discrepant findings, and agreement between caregiver and self-report has rarely been examined <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Giménez et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Horne et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While self-report in individuals with DS is limited by variability in comprehension and acquiescence, many individuals with DS demonstrate relative strengths that may support meaningful participation in appropriately adapted self-report measures (Antonarakis et al., 2020; Finlay & Lyons, 2022).
text.formatted: While self-report in individuals with DS is limited by variability in comprehension and acquiescence, many individuals with DS demonstrate relative strengths that may support meaningful participation in appropriately adapted self-report measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Antonarakis et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Finlay & Lyons, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, self-report might be both feasible and informative when assessment tools are appropriately adapted and results are interpreted alongside proxyreports (Mumbardó-Adam et al., 2023; Roll & Koehly, 2020; Scott & Havercamp, 2018).
text.formatted: Therefore, self-report might be both feasible and informative when assessment tools are appropriately adapted and results are interpreted alongside proxyreports <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Mumbardó-Adam et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Roll & Koehly, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Scott & Havercamp, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, little is known about the concordance of self-and caregiver-reports of sleep problems in young people with DS.
Thus, examining agreement between these perspectives may help inform how sleep is assessed in DS.

This study addresses these gaps by examining the prevalence of sleep problems, age and sex differences, and agreement between self-and caregiver-reports among adolescents and young adults with DS through two preliminary studies.
Study 1 examines the prevalence of caregiver-reported sleep problems among young people with DS and their associations with age and sex.
Study 2 examines caregiver-reported and self-reported sleep problems and patterns in children and adults with DS, focusing on differences and agreement between these informants.
Together, these studies help characterize sleep problems in young people with DS across development and inform how to best evaluate them in future research and practice.
Both studies received Institutional Review Board approval, and written informed consent from parents or legal guardians and assent from participants with Down syndrome was obtained.

The sample included 24 participants with DS (37% female, Mage=18.33 years, SD=4.38; range=12-28 years) and their caregivers (79% mothers, 17% fathers, 4% other; Mage=50.16 years, SD=13.50; age range=21-65 years) recruited from local clinics and organizations serving individuals with DS.

Using Qualtrics, a secure, web-based platform, caregivers answered six dichotomous questions (0=no,1=yes) assessing if the individual with DS experienced bedtime resistance, prolonged sleep onset latency, inappropriate sleep location, nighttime awakenings, early morning awakenings, and daytime sleepiness.
For each sleep problem, prevalence was estimated with frequencies, and relations with child age and sex were tested with binomial logistic regressions.
Results from descriptive analyses are presented in Figure 1.
text.formatted: Results from descriptive analyses are presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>.

text.text: Daytime sleepiness had the highest prevalence, with 92% (n=22) of caregivers endorsing this problem for their child.
Bedtime resistance was the second highest at 79% (n=19), followed by nighttime awakenings at 75% (n=18).

Finally, 58% (n=14) of caregivers reported their child experiencing prolonged sleep onset latency, 54% (n=13) reported their child experiencing early morning awakenings, and 46% (n=11) reported their child sleeping in an inappropriate sleep location.
Results from binomial logistic regressions revealed that older age was associated with increased odds of experiencing prolonged sleep onset latency (see Table 1).
text.formatted: Results from binomial logistic regressions revealed that older age was associated with increased odds of experiencing prolonged sleep onset latency (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Neither age nor sex significantly predicted other sleep problems.
Interactions between age and sex were also tested for each sleep problem, though none of the interactions reached significance (see Table 1).
text.formatted: Interactions between age and sex were also tested for each sleep problem, though none of the interactions reached significance (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: For this sample, internal consistency for the five-item subscales was α=.23 and .73 for Restless Legs and α=.72 and .88 for Insomnia for self-and caregiver-report, respectively.
For two-item subscales, the inter-item correlation is reported rather than Cronbach's alpha because alpha is strongly influenced by the number of items.
Bedtime Fears/Worries inter-item correlations were r=-.41 for self-report and r=.36 for caregiver-report, indicating that self-report responses to the items did not covary in the expected direction.
The two items were scored in the same direction in the original CRSP measure by Meltzer et al. (2013), suggesting that the negative association was not attributable to reverse coding.
text.formatted: The two items were scored in the same direction in the original CRSP measure by <ref type="bibr">Meltzer et al. (2013)</ref>, suggesting that the negative association was not attributable to reverse coding.

text.text: Parasomnias inter-item correlations were r=.48 for self-report and r=.32 for caregiver-report.
Missing items (0.21% for caregivers and 1.25% for self-report) were imputed using the respondent's mean of remaining items in that index before computing the composite scores.
Given distributional assumptions for parametric tests were not consistently met (Shapiro-Wilk test of normality ps ranged from <.001 to .506), nonparametric analyses were conducted.
text.formatted: Given distributional assumptions for parametric tests were not consistently met (Shapiro-Wilk test of normality ps ranged from <.001 to .506), nonparametric analyses were conducted.

text.text: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests compared caregiver and self-reports across CRSP indices and sleeppattern variables.

Two-way mixed-effects, single-measure, absolute-agreement ICCs were used to assess caregiver-child agreement, and Spearman rank-order correlations were used to evaluate associations between reporters.
Given the small sample size, effect sizes were interpreted alongside statistical significance.
Effect sizes for Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were calculated as r = |Z|/√N, where Z represents the standardized test statistic and N represents the number of nonzero paired differences.
Values of approximately .10, .30, and .50 were interpreted as small, moderate, and large effects, respectively, with larger values indicating greater magnitudes of paired differences.
Paired-samples Cohen's d (dz) was also calculated by dividing the mean within-dyad difference by the standard deviation of those differences.
Descriptive statistics and caregiver-child agreement on the CRSP are summarized in Table 2.
text.formatted: Descriptive statistics and caregiver-child agreement on the CRSP are summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>.

text.text: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests revealed significant differences between caregiver and selfreports on five measures.

Individuals with DS reported higher scores than caregivers for Sleep Location (r=.89, dz=.99, p=.012), Bedtime Fears/Worries (r=.80, dz=.83 p=.023), Restless Legs (r=.89, dz=1.11, p=.007), Insomnia (r=.77, dz=.82, p=.014) and enuresis (r=.91, dz=.67, p=.041).
Wilcoxon effect sizes were large (r=.77-.91), while Cohen's dz values indicated moderate to large standardized mean differences (.67-1.11).
No significant caregiver-participant differences were observed for the remaining subscales or items (all ps>.05).
text.formatted: No significant caregiver-participant differences were observed for the remaining subscales or items (all ps>.05).

text.text: Effect sizes ranged from r=.05 to .65, indicating negligible to large effects, Cohen's dz values ranged from .00 to .58, indicating negligible to moderate effects.
Absolute agreement was generally low across indices, subscales, and items.

ICCs ranged from -.26 to .71, with the strongest agreement observed for Weekend Bedtime (ICC=.71, 95% CI [.23, .91]), Weekend Wake Time (ICC=.54, 95% CI [.04, .84]) and Caffeine (ICC=.55, 95% CI [.02, .85]).
Spearman rank-order correlations indicated a significant strong, positive association between caregiver and self-reports for Weekend Bedtime (ρ=.803, p=.002).
Associations for remaining sleep pattern variables were nonsignificant (all ps>.05), with coefficients ranging from ρ=-.22 to .58, reflecting weak negative to moderate positive associations.
text.formatted: Associations for remaining sleep pattern variables were nonsignificant (all ps>.05), with coefficients ranging from ρ=-.22 to .58, reflecting weak negative to moderate positive associations.

text.text: The present studies yielded two primary findings.

First, young people with DS exhibited high rates of sleep problems including daytime sleepiness, bedtime resistance, and nighttime awakenings, with older individuals having a greater likelihood of experiencing prolonged sleep onset latency.

Second, individuals with DS and their caregivers demonstrate limited agreement across most sleep domains, with significant differences observed for several CRSP measures and significant agreement found only for weekend bedtime.
Results of Study 1 build on the limited literature examining sleep problems in adolescents and young adults with DS.

The most prevalent sleep problems experienced by individuals with DS as reported by their caregivers included daytime sleepiness, bedtime resistance, and nighttime awakenings, while prolonged sleep onset latency, early morning awakenings, and inappropriate sleep location were less frequently endorsed.

In a prior study of sleep problems reported by 101 caregivers of individuals with DS aged 16-61 years (Stores, 2019), individuals with DS were reported to experience lower rates of excessive daytime sleepiness (73%), bedtime resistance (49%), nighttime awakenings (59%), and early morning awakenings (41%) occurring at least monthly, but a higher rate of prolonged sleep onset latency (64%).
text.formatted: In a prior study of sleep problems reported by 101 caregivers of individuals with DS aged 16-61 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Stores, 2019)</ref>, individuals with DS were reported to experience lower rates of excessive daytime sleepiness (73%), bedtime resistance (49%), nighttime awakenings (59%), and early morning awakenings (41%) occurring at least monthly, but a higher rate of prolonged sleep onset latency (64%).

text.text: In contrast, results of the current study, which reflect rates of sleep problems in a younger sample, suggest that some sleep problems, such as daytime sleepiness, bedtime resistance, and nighttime awakenings, occur more frequently among adolescents and young adults with DS compared to older individuals.

Findings from Study 1 also revealed that older adolescents and young adults with DS were more likely to experience prolonged sleep onset latency, aligning with prior research in children with DS, which found that sleep onset delay increased with children's age (Maris et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Findings from Study 1 also revealed that older adolescents and young adults with DS were more likely to experience prolonged sleep onset latency, aligning with prior research in children with DS, which found that sleep onset delay increased with children's age <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Maris et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Across development, pubertal changes have been associated with maturational shifts in sleep, suggesting that many sleep problems may have a biological underpinning (Carskadon, 1993).
text.formatted: Across development, pubertal changes have been associated with maturational shifts in sleep, suggesting that many sleep problems may have a biological underpinning <ref type="bibr">(Carskadon, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Increased environmental demands associated with aging (e.g., completing traditional schooling) may also contribute to sleep problems.
Such phenomena have been observed in typically developing young people (Lecarie et al., 2022) but less is known about how these developmental changes influence sleep among young people with DS.
text.formatted: Such phenomena have been observed in typically developing young people <ref type="bibr">(Lecarie et al., 2022)</ref> but less is known about how these developmental changes influence sleep among young people with DS.

text.text: Thus, future research should investigate mechanisms underlying age-related sleep problems in young people with DS, including pubertal changes in adolescence or stress associated with leaving school or entering the work force in early adulthood, to help inform the most targeted and developmentally appropriate interventions.

Although age and sex did not predict other sleep problems in the current study, the small sample size may have limited the ability to detect small effects, warranting larger and more adequately powered studies to clarify age-and sex-related patterns of sleep difficulties in youth with DS.
Results of Study 2 build on the limited literature examining differences and agreement between self-and caregiver-reported sleep in individuals with DS.

Individuals with DS reported significantly higher levels of sleep location difficulties, bedtime fears, restless legs, insomnia, and enuresis than caregivers, with all five differences showing large effects.
Notably, this pattern is the opposite of what a positive self-report bias would predict; rather than minimizing problems, youth with DS endorsed more sleep concerns than their caregivers.
Together, these findings suggest that caregiver and self-reports provide complementary rather than interchangeable information.

Consistent with prior research, discrepancies between self-and proxy-reports may reflect differences between observable sleep patterns and more subjective sleep experiences (Scott & Havercamp, 2018; Roll & Koehly, 2020).
text.formatted: Consistent with prior research, discrepancies between self-and proxy-reports may reflect differences between observable sleep patterns and more subjective sleep experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Scott & Havercamp, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Roll & Koehly, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Differences in insomnia, bedtime fears, and restless legs may reflect subjective experiences that are less observable to caregivers.
However, these differences should be interpreted cautiously given the poor internal consistency observed for some self-report subscales.
The Restless Legs subscale demonstrated low internal consistency (α=.23), while the two Bedtime Fears/Worries items were negatively correlated (r=-.41).
These findings suggest that discrepancies between caregiver-and self-reports may partly reflect measurement limitations rather than differences in sleep experiences alone.
Although visual supports and interviewer assistance were provided, further modifications to item wording or administration procedures may be necessary.
Future research should evaluate the reliability and validity of such adaptations.
Associations and absolute agreement between reporters were generally limited, although stronger correspondence was observed for some sleep-schedule variables, particularly Weekend Bedtime.
These findings support a multi-informant approach in which caregiver-and self-reports provide complementary perspectives on sleep.

At the same time, the inclusion of self-report measures, with appropriate supports aligns with broader efforts to promote more inclusive and person-centered assessment practices in research involving individuals with ID.
Findings underscore the complexity of sleep assessment in individuals with DS and emphasize the need for continued research using multi-method approaches, though several limitations should be noted.
The modest sample size and broad age range across both studies limited statistical power and generalizability, particularly for detecting concordance across informants.
An additional limitation is the weaker psychometric properties of some CRSP selfreport subscales, particularly Bedtime Fears/Worries and Restless Legs.
Findings from these subscales should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

Additionally, sleep outcomes were based on self-report and caregiver-report rather than objective measures such as actigraphy or polysomnography, limiting conclusions about which reporter's information more accurately reflected participants' sleep.
Future research should incorporate objective sleep measures alongside both informants.

The high prevalence of daytime sleepiness, bedtime resistance, and nighttime awakenings among young people with DS and the increased likelihood of prolonged sleep onset latency with age highlight the importance of regular monitoring of sleep problems.
Further, the limited concordance between caregiver-and self-report measures of sleep problems underscores the need for multi-informant assessment approaches in both research and clinical settings.

Integrating caregiver-report, self-report, and objective measures may improve identification of sleep problems and support more targeted, individualized interventions, reinforcing the value of inclusive sleep assessment strategies.

text.text: The data used for this study are available upon request to the corresponding author.
The authors reported there are no conflicts of interest to declare.

Twelve individuals with DS (25% female, Mage=29.17 years, SD=8.99; range=13-43 years) and their caregivers (75% mothers, 17% sisters, and 8% stepmothers) were recruited from a local organization serving individuals with ID.
Participants with DS were predominantly White (75%), with 17% identifying as Black and 8% as Asian.
Participants with DS completed questionnaires individually with trained research assistants at the local organization; items were read aloud, and visual supports aided comprehension.
Caregivers completed questionnaires online via Qualtrics.

Sleep patterns and sleep-related problems were assessed using the Children's Report of Sleep Patterns (CRSP; Meltzer et al., 2013), a 60-item questionnaire that includes parallel selfand caregiver-report forms.
The CRSP consists of three modules: Sleep Patterns, the Sleep Hygiene Index, and the Sleep Disturbance Scale.
The Sleep Patterns module assesses weekday and weekend sleep schedules, sleep latency, sleep duration, nighttime awakenings, and sleep quality, as well as snoring, nightmares, and enuresis.
The Sleep Hygiene Index assesses caffeine use, activities before bed, sleep location, and electronic use before bedtime.
Lastly, the Sleep Disturbance Scale assesses bedtime fears/worries, restless leg symptoms, parasomnias, and insomnia-related symptoms.

Consistent with the measure developers' guidelines, internal consistency was evaluated only for the Sleep Disturbances subscales because the Sleep Hygiene and Sleep Patterns modules consist of distinct indicators not expected to reflect a single underlying construct(Meltzer et al., 2013).

The CRSP has demonstrated low to acceptable internal consistency for the Sleep Disturbance Scale subscales (Cronbach's α=.64-.76) and good test-retest reliability and construct validity in normative samples(Meltzer et al., 2013).
Although developed for pediatric populations, the CRSP was selected because it includes parallel caregiver-and self-report forms across multiple sleep domains.
